findings.title: `check/filter` substitutes placeholders inside a value taken from the caller's header, so a header of a few hundred bytes grows the filter text by its fifth power and can run the agent out of memory
findings.problem: After the first pass, `substitute` runs `placeholderRE` four more times over the whole output, which by then holds the rendered values of HEADER and TOKEN PIPs. A request header that a HEADER PIP reads is caller-controlled, so a caller can put `${…}` into it. With a predicate that names that HEADER PIP, a header holding k copies of `${subject.h}` grows to about k^5 copies: 20 copies (240 bytes) give a 77 MB answer, and about 30 copies (360 bytes) give more than the 700Mi memory limit of the dev profiles. Fiber accepts headers of several KiB, so one request can end the process. This breaks the repository rule that time and memory per request stay linear in the caller's bytes and that input too big fails the request, not the process. The same re-substitution lets a header name any other placeholder: `${resourceType}` in the header comes back as `doc`, and `${subject.<general pip>}` makes the agent call that PIP with its own token and write the answer into the filter text.

reproducer.code:
// package snapshot, beside filter_test.go
set := `{"policySetId": "s", "name": "s", "status": "ACTIVE", "tenantId": "t",
	"target": "resourceType == 'doc'", "combiningAlgorithm": "DENY_UNLESS_PERMIT",
	"policies": [{"policyId": "p", "target": "true", "combiningAlgorithm": "DENY_UNLESS_PERMIT", "tenantId": "t",
		"rules": [{"ruleId": "allow", "target": "true", "effect": "ALLOW", "tenantId": "t",
			"rsqlPredicate": "a==${subject.h}"}]}]}`
pips := `{"tenantId": "t", "name": "subject.h", "pipType": "HEADER", "header": "X-H"}`
r := New(Config{}, tab(t), quiet{})
load(t, r, pips, set)
op := "read"
a, _ := r.Filter(context.Background(), FilterRequest{Tenant: "t", ResourceType: "doc", Operation: &op,
	Headers: map[string]string{"x-h": strings.Repeat("${subject.h}", 20)}})
// current: a.Conditions["rsql"] is 77 MB long, after 3 s and 440 MB RSS
// expected: a=="${subject.h}${subject.h}…" (the header as written, 240 bytes), or DENY

evidence.text: internal/regogen/filtersub.go:128-135: `out := placeholderRE.ReplaceAllStringFunc(strings.ReplaceAll(text, "$${", "\x00{"), one)` then `for range 4 { again := placeholderRE.ReplaceAllStringFunc(out, one) ... out = again }`. The later passes run over the substituted values, not only over the policy's template.

internal/regogen/filtersub.go:195-206: a HEADER PIP takes its value from `headerPIP(decl, s.req.Headers)`, and a TOKEN PIP from `tokenPIP(decl, s.req.Claims)`. `renderValue` (:338-374) copies each item into the text without escaping it.

I ran this in a test in package snapshot at c8315157: one ALLOW rule with `"rsqlPredicate": "a==${subject.h}"` and `"sqlPredicate": "a = ${subject.h}"`, a HEADER PIP `subject.h` on `X-H`, and `Registry.Filter` with header `x-h`. These header lengths gave these answer lengths: 24 bytes (2 copies) → 943, 36 bytes (3) → 6367, 72 bytes (6) → 192895, 240 bytes (20) → 77473735. The 20-copy run peaked at 440 MB RSS. The header `${resourceType}` gave `a=="doc"` and `a = 'doc'`.
Growth is about 24·k^5 bytes, so 30 copies (360 bytes) give about 580 MB of text plus the intermediate strings of each pass, and 300 copies (3.6 KB) cannot finish.

kichasov's review of 2026-11-05 lists "`filtersub.go:338` writes values into predicates without escaping" as existing behavior for its own issue. That note is about one value widening the predicate. It does not cover a value being substituted again, which is what makes the size grow without bound and lets the caller trigger PIP calls.

`source` (filtersub.go:153-221) resolves any `subject.<name>` that `s.m.pips` knows, so a header holding `${subject.g}` reaches `generalValue` and calls GENERAL PIP g with the agent's token, even when no predicate of the request names g.

findings.proposed_solution: Owner decision: Fix now: a defect in regogen's substitution of HEADER and TOKEN values, not a token question. Substitute only the placeholders written in the policy's template, once: a value from a source is final text and is never scanned again, so the output is linear in the template and the values, and a header or claim can no longer name another placeholder. Keep `$${x}` in the template as the text `${x}`. The owner decided this as a deliberate departure from legacy: legacy re-substitutes inside values (golden id44-template-0), so the agent's answer to that golden changes from the subject id to the literal `${subject.id}`.
findings.retest: A filter request whose HEADER PIP header holds `strings.Repeat("${subject.h}", 300)` finishes in milliseconds with that header text rendered once, as is. A header `${resourceType}` comes back as the literal `${resourceType}`. A GENERAL PIP answering `["${subject.id}"]` renders `a=in=("${subject.id}")`. `$${subject.x}` in the template still renders as `${subject.x}`.

findings.title: A bulk/operations item decodes, copies, and projects its resource once per operation, so a 266 KB body with 100 operations allocates 1.6 GB and holds 1.2 GB live before any policy runs
findings.problem: Work and memory grow as (number of operations) x (resource bytes), both from one untrusted body, which breaks the AGENTS.md rule that a request stays linear in the caller's bytes. With the 32 MiB body limit, one request can exhaust a replica's memory (the dev profiles limit it to 700Mi) or hold a worker for tens of seconds. Since this change an empty operation `""` is decided rather than skipped, so each extra copy costs 3 bytes of body.

evidence.text: components/authz-agent/internal/legacy/legacy.go:310 `r, err := newResource(typ, op, res)` runs inside `for _, op := range ops`, and newResource decodes `res` again each time through `value(res, map[string]any{})` (legacy.go:361-369, `util.UnmarshalJSON(raw, &v)`).

components/authz-agent/internal/server/decide.go:259-264 calls `body(r.Raw)` for every Resource, and `body` runs `jsonvalue.Decode(raw.Resource)` (decide.go:316), so the same resource text is decoded a second time per operation.

Measured in a separate worktree at c8315157 with the reproducer: the parse in package legacy alone allocated 836 MB for n=100 and the snapshotRequest decoding added about 760 MB; after GC the live heap was 1217 MB for a 266 KB body.

components/authz-agent/internal/regogen/bulk.go: `Item` gives every item `docs: regobuiltins.NewDocuments()` and `value` converts `in.resource` with `in.docs.Term(in.resource)`, so the evaluation converts the same resource to an OPA term once more per operation, and `admit` passes all copies to the admission query (decide.go:124).
legacy.go:306 `if s := string(bytes.TrimSpace(op)); s == "" || s == "null"` now skips only null; before this change `name == ""` skipped an empty-string operation too.

At 659df567, expand already called newResource(typ, nil, res) once per operation (legacy.go:278-291), so the parse was quadratic before; the change adds the snapshotRequest decode and the projection per operation, and makes an empty operation count.

findings.title: A load that changes a PIP's requestAttributes from absent to {} keeps the old snapshot, so the PIP keeps receiving a null body until the agent restarts
findings.problem: The registry reuses a tenant's snapshot whenever the sha256 of Tree.Dump() is unchanged, but Dump is a golden-file rendering that is not injective: it prints requestAttributes only when the map is non-empty, while the generator sends `null` for a nil map and `{}` for an empty one. After a PAP edit that adds `"requestAttributes": {}` (or removes it), the load reports the tenant as kept and the agent keeps calling the PIP with the old body; a freshly started agent sends the new one. The answer of a PIP that reads its body, and every decision over it, then depends on whether the agent restarted since the edit.

evidence.text: components/authz-agent/internal/snapshot/registry.go:379-383: `sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(tree.Dump()))` ... `if old, ok := prev.snapshots[t]; ok && old.treeKey == treeKey {` / `b.snap, b.kept = old, true`

internal/policyir/dump.go:140: `if len(p.RequestAttributes) > 0 {` — nil and empty maps print the same text; internal/policyir/tree.go:253-256 documents that nil and {} are distinct ("empty for {}, which a call sends as written").
internal/regogen/pipcall.go:157-158: `body := ast.NullTerm()` / `if decl.RequestAttributes != nil {` — the request body is null for nil and an object for {}.

Ran a probe test in components/authz-agent/internal/snapshot (pipRegistry, load, decide helpers): load 1 without requestAttributes, load 2 with `"requestAttributes": {}`, then a fresh registry loaded with load 2's documents. Output: `load2 {Tenants:1 Generated:0 Compiled:0 Kept:1 ...}`, PIP bodies received `["{\"requestAttributes\":null}" "{\"requestAttributes\":null}" "{\"requestAttributes\":{}}"]` — the reloaded registry still sends null, the fresh one sends {}.
The reverse edit ({} to absent) is kept the same way, since both dumps are equal.

kichasov's review of 2026-11-05 (raw/reviews.md) lists the same case among its non-blocking decisions ("requestAttributes null and {} give one tree key ... so a running agent keeps the old body"); no reply followed, and the probe above shows it still holds at c8315157.

findings.proposed_solution: The decision to reuse a snapshot rests on a key that must identify everything Generate and the module's Go side read from the tree, and Dump was written for golden files, not for that. Key the snapshot on a canonical serialization that keeps every field and the nil/empty distinction (for example the JSON of the tree, or the generated module plus the PIP declarations it carries), or make Dump print `requestAttributes={}` for an empty map and state in its doc comment that equal text means equal trees, with a test that pins it.
findings.retest: A load whose only change is a PIP's requestAttributes going from absent to {} regenerates the tenant (LoadSummary.Generated == 1) and the next call of the PIP carries the body {"requestAttributes":{}}; the reverse edit ({} to absent) makes the next call carry null.

findings.title: A PIP that answers 200 with a body that is not JSON reads as PIP_NULL, so a DENY over it does not fire
findings.problem: An outage page served with 200 (`<html>`, `{`, `x`) turns off DENY rules on `==`, MATCH, CONTAINS, IS NOT NULL, and IN over that PIP, on check/resource and in the filter. `main` takes a value only from a body that is valid JSON. The goldens q15-a-text-body-* read such a body as null too, so the fix deliberately departs from those goldens, as the owner has chosen: a body that does not parse as JSON is an error.

evidence.text: internal/regogen/pipcall.go:509-510 `// a body that is not JSON reads as a JSON string body does` / `body = string(raw)`
internal/regogen/pipcall.go:537-538 `// an object or a string as the whole body reads as a null body` / `return Resolved{State: spectables.StatePIPNull}, nil`
kichasov 2026-11-18 reproduced the DENY not firing for `x`, `<html>`, `{`, and an empty 200 body at c8315157

golden q15-a-text-body-*: pip-mock answers 200 with the raw body `v`; an ALLOW `subject.parityR15Text == 'v' OR resource.a == 'y'` allows when `resource.a` is `y` and denies otherwise, and `IS NULL` over the PIP holds, so the golden reads the body as null and does not fail the request
engine.py general_value in the specification cites q15-a-text-body-* for `a body that is not JSON reads as a JSON string body does`, the reading pipcall.go:509-510 copies
a response with zero bytes (204, or 200 with an empty body) has no golden; round 15 pinned the JSON body `null` (r15-null-body), not an empty one

findings.proposed_solution: Read a non-empty PIP body that does not decode as JSON as a failed source (ERROR), the state a failed call or a status other than 200 and 204 already gets. This departs from the goldens q15-a-text-body-*, which read such a body as null, and the owner has chosen the departure: a JSON parse error is an error. Record it where the project records deliberate departures from the parity goldens, and make the parity expectations for q15-a-text-body-* expect the agent's answer, not the golden. Fix the class, not the four reported inputs: the rule covers any body that fails to decode, including truncated JSON, whitespace only, an HTML page from a proxy, and content-encoded bytes, which also removes F16. Apply it at every place that decodes a PIP response body: pipResolve for GENERAL and FILTERED, the entitlements service, and the permission scope. Search for every decode that falls back to treating the raw bytes as a string, and remove the fallback. Keep two readings unchanged. A body that decodes as JSON keeps the state the specification gives it, including an object or a string as the whole body (pipcall.go:537-538), which the goldens q15-an-object-body-* and ok-general-string-* back. A response with zero bytes (204, or 200 with an empty body) still reads as a null body; decoding zero bytes must not fall into the new ERROR branch. The ERROR is logged and traced the way a failed call is, and the log names the PIP and the status, not the body.
findings.retest: A DENY `subject.g == 'x'` beside an ALLOW, the PIP answering 200 with `<html>`: check/resource denies with `PIP resolution failed: subject.g`, and check/filter answers DENY. The same holds for `{`, `x`, a whitespace-only body, and a body with `Content-Encoding: br`, for a PIP with and without jsonPath, and for the entitlements service and the permission scope. Negative controls: a 204 and a 200 with zero bytes still read as PIP_NULL (the DENY on `==` does not fire, IS NULL holds); a 200 with the JSON body `"x"` or `{"k": "v"}` keeps its current state.

findings.title: Does `subject.isM2M`, bare or in a comparison, read the M2M test as ADR-0092 R10 says? A comparison reads ABSENT for every caller, and the bare reading uses another test than the tenant check
findings.problem: A DENY rule `subject.isM2M == true` never denies a service account, while a bare `subject.isM2M` does; the ADR in this repository says every reader reads the result of the M2M test. When a request carries no Incoming-Token, one token is both caller and subject, and the two tests disagree: `level: key-manager` or `ROLE_M2M` lets the caller reach any tenant while a bare `subject.isM2M` is false and `subject.type` USER; `preferred_username: service-account-x` gives `subject.isM2M` true while the caller stays limited to its `tenant-id` tenant.

evidence.text: internal/regogen/local.go:83-84 `case spectables.KindPIPMapping, spectables.KindSubjIsM2M:` / `v = Resolved{State: spectables.StateAbsent}`
docs/decisions/20261029-authz-agent-adr-0092-tokens-in-authorization.md:81 `**R10** (handler, policy). Every reader, subject.isM2M among them, reads that result.`

components/authz-agent/internal/server/decide.go:173-184: `m2mToken` holds for `level` equal to `m2m` or `key-manager` without regard to case (`strings.EqualFold(level, "m2m") || strings.EqualFold(level, "key-manager")`), or for `ROLE_M2M` in `realm_access.roles`. `callerMayReach` (:153) uses it to let a caller reach any tenant.

internal/regogen/subject.go:134: `s.M2M = typ == "SERVICE" || t.levelM2M()`. `service()` (:187-193) holds for `preferred_username` starting with `service-account-` or for `levelM2M()`, and `levelM2M()` (:196-199) holds only for `level` equal to `m2m` in any case. Neither reads `key-manager` or `ROLE_M2M`.

components/authz-agent/internal/snapshot/decide.go:91 and snapshot/filter.go:64 compute the subject with `regogen.SubjectOf(claims, ...)` from the claims alone, and pass no M2M result from the admission. server/decide.go:63 and :92 pass `admission["tokenPayload"]` as those claims.

docs/decisions/20261029-authz-agent-adr-0092-tokens-in-authorization.md:72-81 (R6, R21, R9, R10) define the test as R6 or R21 and require one computation that every reader, `subject.isM2M` among them, reads. The record is Proposed.

The executable specification defines the bare reading as SERVICE or level m2m, which c72-m2m-level-m2m and r43open-m2m-level-* record, and ADR-0092 is Proposed, so whether R10 or the specification's reading governs is the owner's call.

findings.proposed_solution:
Owner decision: Split. The comparison half is settled by the goldens and needs a test and a load warning now. The bare-reading half (which claims make a token M2M, and whether subject.isM2M reads the caller check's result) is deferred to the token pull requests (#279, #292, #329, #332, and #338 of Netcracker/qubership-authz-agent, which rework ADR-0091 to ADR-0096 and the agent's token source). In this change: keep the ABSENT reading of a comparison over subject.isM2M. The goldens TestRound11DeclaredNameCases/dm-is-m2m-declared and dm-is-m2m-undeclared load `subject.isM2M == 'yes'` with 200 and decide false with the header set to yes, which is what ABSENT gives an ALLOW rule. Pin it: a test that cites those cases and asserts the ALLOW decides false, and a test that a DENY over `subject.isM2M == true` does not deny, marked as having no golden. Have the load log a warning that names the policy and says the comparison never holds and subject.isM2M is written as a bare condition. Do not change `m2mToken`, `callerMayReach`, `SubjectOf`, `service`, or `levelM2M`.
Separate change: after the token pull requests merge, compute the M2M test once, where the token is verified, as the reworked ADR-0092 defines it, and have the caller check and SubjectOf read that result. When Incoming-Token is present the caller and the subject are two tokens, so the two readings may still differ there; the regular/it72-* goldens record such requests.
findings.retest: In this change: a test cites dm-is-m2m-declared and dm-is-m2m-undeclared and asserts that an ALLOW over `subject.isM2M == 'yes'` decides false; a test asserts that a DENY over `subject.isM2M == true` does not deny; the load logs a warning that names the policy. The tests of m2mToken and SubjectOf are unchanged. The bare-reading half is not retested in this change.

findings.title: The filter writes a veto text derived from the condition, which admits rows `==` would match (case, number as string), where ADR-0099 R14 writes none

findings.title: A subject operand that is neither a built-in attribute, a permission scope key, nor a declared PIP is read from the resource instead of being refused at load
findings.problem: `subject.roles[0] == 'admin'` is satisfied by `{"subject":{"roles":["admin"]}}` in the resource, and the tenant reports ready with no failure. An author who writes it expects the token's roles. The same silent resource reading applies to every `subject.` token that the PIP-name pattern does not match: `subject.l[0]`, `subject.x-y`, `subject.1x`, `subject.a.` with a trailing dot. The agent matches the goldens here: k19-063…k19-070 read such an operand from the resource, while p47-o124/write-1 refuses a plain dotted `subject.<name>` that is neither a built-in attribute nor a declared PIP. No golden gives `subject.<x>[i]` the meaning of a token attribute. No policy in the production corpus uses such an operand.

evidence.text: internal/policyir/parse.go:634 `return p.resource("."+path, tok, dot), nil`
internal/policyir/operand.go:47-50 `a subject token that is neither a built-in attribute, a PIP name, nor subject.permissionScope.<key>, are resource paths too`

Parity goldens k19-063…k19-070 (PR #42): `subject.l[0] IS NULL` is true and every other comparison with it is false for a resource without a `subject` field, so the goldens read `subject.l[0]` from the resource.

Parity golden load-policy-sets-v1/sequence/p47-o124/write-1 (PR #42): the golden refuses a policy set whose condition is `subject.parityUnknown == 'x'` with 400 and `Invalid expression: subject.parityUnknown PIP doesn't exist`.
Owner decision in the thread: refuse such operands at load rather than keep the resource reading the goldens record.

findings.proposed_solution:
Owner decision: refuse at load. Implement it as one general rule, not as a special case for `[`: an operand that starts with `subject.` always reads the subject, and a policy whose `subject.` operand is not a built-in subject attribute, not `subject.permissionScope.<key>`, and not a declared PIP is refused at load.

1. In `internal/policyir/parse.go`, drop the branch of the subject-token handling that turns a non-PIP `subject.` token into a resource path (`return p.resource("."+path, tok, dot), nil`). Return a refusal instead, through the same path that refuses an unsupported jsonPath (an `Unsupported` operand with a new form, or a parse error, whichever that path already uses), so the policy lands in the tenant's `Failures` and the load logs a warning. Cover every token shape the PIP-name pattern rejects: brackets, `-`, a segment that starts with a digit, a trailing dot, and the right side of `MATCH`.
2. The error names the policy and the operand as written, and gives the fix: to read the resource, write `resource.subject.roles[0]`; to test the token's roles, write `subject.roles CONTAINS 'admin'`.
3. Update the comment on `Resource` in `internal/policyir/operand.go:47-50`, which says such subject tokens are resource paths. A path written without the `resource` prefix stays a resource path; only the `subject.` case changes.
4. This deliberately departs from the goldens k19-063…k19-070. Record it in the project's list of deliberate departures from the parity goldens, cite those goldens, and mark those cases as an expected difference for the agent, so the parity suite does not report them as failures.
5. Tests: one parser or load test per token shape in step 1, each asserting the refusal and its message; a negative control showing that `subject.roles`, `subject.permissionScope.k`, and a declared PIP `subject.foo` still load; and a test that `resource.subject.l[0]` still reads the resource.
findings.retest: Load a tenant whose policy has `subject.roles[0] == 'admin'`: the policy appears in `Failures` with a message naming it and the operand, the load warns, and a request with `{"subject":{"roles":["admin"]}}` in the resource is not permitted by it. Repeat for `subject.x-y`, `subject.1x`, `subject.a.`, and `resource.v MATCH subject.l[0]`. `subject.roles`, `subject.permissionScope.k`, a declared PIP, and `resource.subject.l[0]` still load.

findings.title: A partial load writes one WARN that joins every refused tenant with its full refusal text, and rewrites all of them whenever any one changes.
findings.problem: The unit here is each tenant's refusal state, but the record is one line per load over all tenants. With many tenants refused (the corpus has 1011 tenants), one line can run to many kilobytes, past the line limit of common log shippers, and a new refusal in one tenant re-emits every unchanged refusal beside it, so the reader cannot tell which tenant changed. The registry already knows per tenant whether a refusal is new (`build.repeat`).

findings.title: What bounds one decision request once a PIP stops answering? Nothing but the item count does: each distinct PIP call waits AUTHZ_PIP_TIMEOUT, items run 4 at a time, and the calls are not cancelled when the caller gives up
findings.problem: With a PIP that accepts connections and never answers, a bulk request whose items send distinct PIP requests (a FILTERED PIP or requestAttributes carrying resource values) is held for about ceil(items/4) x PIPs-per-item x 2 s: 50 items with one such PIP take about 26 s, and a 32 MiB body admits far more items. The caller's own timeout fires long before, yet the agent keeps calling the dead PIP for the abandoned request, so a PIP outage turns into goroutines and connections piling up behind callers that already retried.

evidence.text: components/authz-agent/internal/snapshot/decide.go:93-96: the context is `regobuiltins.WithCalls(ctx)` and `r.cfg.HTTP.Context(ctx)`; no `context.WithTimeout` or deadline is added anywhere on the decision path (grep for Timeout/Deadline in components/authz-agent/internal/server and internal/snapshot finds none outside tests).

components/authz-agent/internal/server/decide.go:48: `ctx := c.UserContext()`; components/authz-agent/main.go:124-141 builds both Fiber servers with no ReadTimeout or WriteTimeout, and Fiber's UserContext is context.Background unless a handler sets one, which public.go:71 does only to attach the request id.

internal/regobuiltins/httpsend.go:332: `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, timeout)` bounds each call alone; a failed call is reused only for an equal request (httpsend.go:187-206), so distinct per-item requests each wait the full timeout.
components/authz-agent/internal/snapshot/registry.go:127-128: `BulkWorkers` defaults to 4; decide.go:142 starts `min(r.cfg.BulkWorkers, len(inputs))` workers.
Since fasthttp does not end the request context when the client disconnects, the PIP calls of an abandoned request run to their own timeouts.

findings.proposed_solution: State the timeout the callers of check/resource, bulk, and check/filter apply, and bound the decision request by a deadline below it (a request budget passed into Decide and Filter, so later PIP calls fail fast once it is spent), or record in the README that a request may wait items/4 x PIPs x AUTHZ_PIP_TIMEOUT.
findings.retest: Settled by an answer naming the callers' timeout and either a request-level deadline at or below it (a bulk request of 50 items, each reading a FILTERED PIP whose server never answers, completes within that deadline with every item denied `PIP resolution failed`), or a written acceptance of the unbounded wait.

findings.title: The corpus replay builds `snapshot.Request` with its own copy of the HTTP projection, so the 122252 matches do not cover how the server builds it
findings.problem: The description says the corpus was "replayed through the service's decision path". The server's projection from an HTTP request to `snapshot.Request` is unexported in package `server` (`snapshotRequest`, `filterRequest`, `claimsOf`), so `snapshot-corpus` and `filter-corpus` each write their own `toRequest`. The copies already differ from the server. A defect in the server's projection, such as a header it drops or passes or a claim that changes on the round trip through the admission result, would not show in the corpus numbers.

evidence.text: components/authz-agent/internal/server/decide.go:251-268: the server takes headers from `legacy.RequestHeaders(headers)`, which drops `authorization`, `incoming-token`, `x-request-id`, and the framing headers (legacy.go:412-417). It sets `IncomingToken` from the header, sets `Anonymous` from `input["subject"] == ""`, and takes claims from `claimsOf(admission["tokenPayload"])`, a `json.Marshal` of the Rego admission result decoded again.

components/authz-agent/cmd/snapshot-corpus/main.go:136-148: `toRequest` lowercases every recorded header and drops none. It sets no `IncomingToken`, takes `Anonymous` from the bundle, and decodes the recorded claims directly. components/authz-agent/cmd/filter-corpus/main.go has a third `toRequest` with the same header and claim handling.
Both tools call `snapshot.Registry.Decide` or `Filter` directly. The code in `server/decide.go` that the service runs before the registry does not run in the replay.

findings.proposed_solution: Owner decision: Fix now. The shared projection carries the claims as the server passes them today; it decides nothing about M2M. Move the projection from headers, resources, and the admission payload to `snapshot.Request` and `snapshot.FilterRequest` into one exported function, for example in package `snapshot` or `legacy`. Have the server and both corpus tools call it. Otherwise, change the description to say that the replay starts at `snapshot.Registry`.
findings.retest: The server and `cmd/snapshot-corpus` build their requests with the same function. Given a recorded request whose headers include `Authorization` and `Incoming-Token`, both produce a `snapshot.Request` without those headers in `Headers` and with `IncomingToken` set.

findings.title: A simplified policy that allows every row returns early, so the veto of a later simplified policy of the same operation whose condition fails is never registered and the filter answers ALLOW where the check denies.
findings.problem: The check denies the resource whenever any applicable simplified policy has a condition over a failed source (`allow if { permit; not failed }`, order-free). The filter registers that veto only for the simplified policies it reaches before the first one whose condition is true without a predicate. With the allowing policy first, check/filter answers ALLOW (every row) while check/resource denies every row with "PIP resolution failed"; with the two policies swapped, the filter answers DENY. The answer depends on the order of the policies in the export, and the filter returns rows the check denies.

evidence.text: internal/regogen/filteralg.go:310-312: `if c.v == 1 { return pair{a: allRows}, nil }` inside the loop over n.simp, after `e.veto(*c.veto)` is called only for the policies already visited (lines 295-298).

The check composes the veto over every applicable node regardless of order: internal/regogen/gen.go:270-272 `anyFailed := union(failed...)` and gen.go:1496-1497 `allow if { permit; not failed }`; simplified policies contribute `k.c.failedU()` for bound E (gen.go:1242-1268).

Ran the reproducer above (in a scratch worktree, as zz_probe_test.go): allow-first gives `filter = {Result:ALLOW}` and `check = [{Allowed:false Reason:PIP resolution failed: subject.g}]`; fail-first gives `filter = {Result:DENY}`.

Neighbor: with the failing policy's condition `subject.g == 'x' AND resource.a == 'y'` (a veto over some rows only), allow-first gives `{Result:ALLOW}` while fail-first gives `USE_FILTER_CONDITION` `a!="y"` / `a <> 'y'`.

The test meant to cover this, TestASimplifiedPolicyOverAFailedSourceDeniesTheRowsWhereItIsUnknown (components/authz-agent/internal/snapshot/filter_test.go:966), puts the allowing policy first but never reaches filterEval.simplified: its rules have target "true", which policyir.simplifiedGroup rejects (rolesOf requires `subject.roles CONTAINS ANY ...`, internal/policyir/export.go:859-866), so the set is loaded as a regular set. An instrumented run printed nothing from filterEval.simplified for that shape.

findings.proposed_solution: Do not return before every simplified policy of the part has been evaluated: record that a policy allows every row, keep going so each matched policy's condition registers its veto, and return allRows after the loop. Make the snapshot test load the set in the shape the PAP writes for simplified policies (rule targets `subject.roles CONTAINS ANY '...'`) so it exercises this path.

findings.title: check/filter answers ALLOW for every row where check/resource denies the rows on which a failed PIP is compared, when the same conjunction holds `subject allowed 'OP' on resource` over a decision with a failed source
findings.problem: `rows` reads every leaf that has no row text, is not in `t`, and is not marked `fails` as false on every row. The leaf of `subject allowed 'write' on resource` whose write decision reads a failed source is three-valued with an empty `failed` rail (`gen.go:845-857` sets only `t`, `f`, `threeValued`), so the filter reads it as false. Kleene AND with false then drops the unknown of the sibling comparison over the failed PIP, `cond` returns no veto, and the filter allows every row. check/resource, through the decision module, denies each row where the comparison reads the failed value (here every row whose `a` is present and not null). This is the fail-open direction of ADR-0098: the filter admits rows that check/resource denies. It is not kichasov's ADR-0099 R3 item (a failed PIP inside the decision of the access leaf keeps a predicate); here no predicate is needed and the failed source is in a sibling atom.

Control: `subject.id == 'x' AND resource.a == subject.h` in place of the access atom gives filter DENY; `subject allowed 'write' on resource` alone, over the same failed write decision, gives check allow on every row and filter ALLOW.

filteralg.go:203-210: `case l.fails && holds(l.key+"e"): v.u = rowsTrue` / `case l.row != nil: ...` / `case holds(l.key): v.t = rowsTrue`; otherwise the leaf stays `{t: rowsFalse, u: rowsFalse}`. filter.go:503-517 sets `fails: !l.failed.isFalse()` per leaf, and the access leaf from gen.go `access` has no `failed` rail.

findings.title: A TOKEN PIP claim that starts with a bracketed key which is not one dotted token, such as $['https://idp/roles'], $['a b'], $['a.b'], or $[''], resolves to ERROR or to the wrong claim, where the specification reads the key as Jayway does.
findings.problem: tokenSelect rewrites a leading ['k'] to .k whatever k holds. A key with a space, a slash, or no characters then fails to compile and the operand is ERROR; a key with a dot reads a nested member instead of the key. Namespaced claims such as https://example.com/roles are written exactly this way, so every condition over such a TOKEN PIP is decided on ERROR or on another claim's value. The same rewrite in pipPath (pipcall.go:81) refuses a GENERAL or FILTERED declaration with such a jsonPath at generation, or reads the nested member for a dotted key.

evidence.text: local.go:201-203: `if m := rootBracket.FindStringSubmatch(path); m != nil { path = "." + m[1] + path[len(m[0]):] }`

Specification engine.py:4194-4205 root_bracket (changed in d444d252 on 2026-11-12, before the head c8315157 of 2026-11-13): `.k when k is one dotted token, else .['k'], so a key with a space, a slash, a dot or no characters stays one key as Jayway reads it (jayway: r75-bracket-space, r75-bracket-slash, r75-bracket-empty)`; the TOKEN branch calls it at engine.py:4528-4530 with p = claim[1:] for a claim starting with $.

Probe run in a worktree at the head: tokenPIP over claims {"a b":"x","a/b":"slash","a.b":"dotted","a":{"b":"nested"},"":"empty"} gives `$['a b'] -> ERROR`, `$['a/b'] -> ERROR`, `$[''] -> ERROR`, `$['a.b'] -> VALUE nested`; the specification gives x, slash, empty, dotted.

The test case "a root bracket read as a key" (local_test.go:80) uses the claim ['a.b'] without $, which tokenSelect prefixes with a dot (".['a.b']") so rootBracket never matches; the diff coverage lists local.go:202 as never executed.
pipcall.go:81-83 applies the same rewrite to a GENERAL or FILTERED jsonPath, and pipcall.go:84-86 turns a compile failure into a rejection of the tenant's declaration.

findings.proposed_solution: Owner decision: Fix now: regogen's reading of a TOKEN PIP's jsonPath, not a question of which tokens are accepted. Make the rewrite the specification's: keep .k only when k is non-empty and reads back as one dotted step of the jsonpath package, and otherwise keep the step as .['k']. Both tokenSelect and pipPath share rootBracket, so fix it once in a helper both call.

findings.title: entResolve removes repeated resource ids with a linear scan per id, so its time grows with the square of the entitlements answer; a 1 MB answer takes 4 s against the 5 ms budget

findings.title: The RSQL parser that negates a DENY predicate recurses once per nested parenthesis with no limit, so a policy predicate of a few megabytes crashes the whole process with a fatal stack overflow on the first filter request.
findings.problem: A goroutine stack overflow is not a recoverable panic: it ends the agent for every tenant, and it recurs on each filter request that renders the negation, so the tenant's policy keeps the service down. The repository rule says input too deep fails its load or request, not the process, and mongoTree applies exactly that bound (jsonvalue.MaxDepth) to MongoDB predicate text for the same reason ("the text comes from a policy and is not bounded by the decoder of the policy around it"). Nothing checks rsqlPredicate at load, and the PAP body may be 32 MiB.

evidence.text: internal/regogen/rsql.go:181-196: or() -> join -> and() -> join -> constraint(), and constraint() calls p.or() again for each LP, with no depth counter.

End-to-end probe in components/authz-agent/internal/snapshot at c8315157: openRule plus a DENY rule whose rsqlPredicate is 3,000,000 `(` + `secret==1` + 3,000,000 `)` (about 6 MB) under DENY_OVERRIDES. load succeeded; filterOf(t, r, "a", "read") ended the test binary with `runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit` / `fatal error: stack overflow` in regogen.(*rsqlParser).join.
components/authz-agent/internal/pull/pull.go:307 reads the PAP response through io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 32<<20).
negateRSQL is called only from negateRSQLTerm (filtertext.go:336), at render time per request, not at load.

findings.proposed_solution: Count the depth in the parser and refuse a text nested deeper than jsonvalue.MaxDepth (negateRSQL then returns false, so the AND drops the RSQL dialect, as for any text it cannot negate), the bound mongoTree already uses. Alternatively reject such a predicate at load with a Rejection; either way negate() and write() recurse over a tree that is then bounded too.
findings.retest: negateRSQL over 3,000,000 nested groups returns false without crashing, and over jsonvalue.MaxDepth groups still negates. Neighbor: the alternating form `a==1;(a==1,(a==1;(...)))` nested as deep must not crash either (same recursion through join), and a filter request with such a DENY predicate answers instead of ending the process.

findings.title: The negation of an RSQL or MongoDB predicate ignores the `$${x}` escape that the predicate itself honours, so the negated text compares with a different value than the DENY predicate does.
findings.problem: substitute turns `$${x}` into the literal text `${x}` and records nothing for it, but negateRSQLTerm and negateMongoLeaf run placeholderRE over the raw template, which matches the `${x}` inside `$${x}`. In RSQL the escaped placeholder is replaced by the value when the same name also appears unescaped, and in MongoDB the doubled `$$` stays. The excluded rows then differ from the rows the DENY predicate names. The same single pass also leaves a placeholder unsubstituted where a value held one, which substitute does replace.

MongoDB template `"a": {"$eq": "$${subject.name}"}`: positive `"a": {"$eq": "${subject.name}"}`, negation `{ "a": {"$ne": "$${subject.name}"} }`.
internal/regogen/filtersub.go:128 and :139 handle the escape (`"$${"` -> `"\x00{"` and back); internal/regogen/filtertext.go:341 and :379 do not.

findings.proposed_solution: Negate the template with the escape protected the same way substitute protects it (replace `$${` before negating, restore it after), and fill each placeholder with the text the positive rendering gave it after all passes, so that both sides go through one substitution routine.
findings.retest: Both negations in the reproducer give the escaped placeholder as the literal `${subject.name}`. Neighbor: a template with only the escaped form (no unescaped use of the name), where RSQL must give `a!=${subject.name}` rather than `a!=$${subject.name}`.

findings.title: Does the RSQL consumer read `*` in an `==` value as a wildcard? A veto written as `a=="y*"` would then keep rows such as a = "yes" that the check denies.

For a condition `resource.a != 'y*'` that a failed source leaves unknown, the veto keeps the rows where a equals the literal and renders `a=="y*"`. RSQL backends in common use (rsql-jpa style) turn `*` in `==` into LIKE, so that text keeps every row starting with y, while the check finds them unequal, unknown, and denies them. The comment above term() assumes the database is stricter than the check; a wildcard makes it looser. SQL and MongoDB compare exactly.

Whether `*` is a wildcard depends on the backend that evaluates rsqlFilterCondition, which is not in this repository.

findings.proposed_solution: If the consumer treats `*` as a wildcard, give no RSQL text to a literal that holds `*` (the veto then falls back to the other dialects or to DENY), as is done for quotes.
findings.retest: Settled by the answer: if `==` with `*` is a wildcard for the consumers, a veto over `resource.a != 'y*'` must not render `a=="y*"`; if it is always an exact match, no change.

classes.title: A bracketed jsonPath key is rewritten to a dotted path
